qs.q: Therapeutic Drug Monitoring (TDM) of vancomycin is used to prevent which complications while ensuring efficacy?
qs.e: Vancomycin trough monitoring (or AUC/MIC-guided dosing) is crucial to avoid nephrotoxicity (associated with high levels) and ototoxicity, while ensuring the drug concentration is sufficient for efficacy (preventing sub-therapeutic levels).

o: Wide therapeutic index and predictable pharmacokinetics

qs.e: TDM is indicated for: narrow therapeutic index drugs (digoxin, lithium, phenytoin, gentamicin, vancomycin, cyclosporine, theophylline), drugs with unpredictable pharmacokinetics, drugs where toxicity mimics the disease being treated, monitoring compliance, and dose adjustment in renal/hepatic failure.

exam: A patient on vancomycin develops rising creatinine – what is the next step? — Check trough level, assess renal function, consider dose reduction or switch to linezolid.
A child with TB is started on isoniazid and rifampicin; you suspect hepatotoxicity – what monitoring is essential? — LFTs every 2 weeks, look for jaundice, consider stopping if AST/ALT >5× ULN.
A patient on azathioprine shows fatigue and mild rash – what drug level should you check? — 6‑MP metabolites; high levels suggest toxicity.
You have a patient on gentamicin with tinnitus – what is the most likely cause and what do you do? — Ototoxicity; stop gentamicin, check trough, consider alternative.
A patient on antiretroviral therapy has poor viral suppression – what TDM test can guide you? — Drug trough level (e.g., lopinavir/ritonavir).
You cannot get a drug assay in a rural clinic – how do you manage a patient on vancomycin? — Monitor trough clinically, adjust dose based on response, ensure adequate hydration.
A patient on vancomycin develops red man syndrome – what is the cause and how do you prevent it? — Rapid infusion; slow infusion over 1–2 hours prevents it.
A patient on linezolid develops thrombocytopenia – what is the likely mechanism? — Inhibition of platelet production; monitor platelets weekly.
ai.title: Therapeutic Drug Monitoring
ai.subject: Pharmacology
ai.summary: Therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) tailors drug dosing by measuring serum levels, ensuring efficacy while avoiding toxicity. It is crucial for drugs with narrow therapeutic indices, especially in low‑resource settings where clinical signs may be subtle.

sections.p: TDM is the systematic measurement of a drug’s plasma concentration to guide dosing. It is indicated when a drug has a narrow therapeutic index, variable pharmacokinetics, or when clinical response is unpredictable.

Severity is judged by the deviation from the therapeutic range: sub‑therapeutic, therapeutic, or supra‑therapeutic. Staging is not formal but clinicians use the magnitude of deviation to decide urgency of dose adjustment.
In low‑resource hospitals, common causes of abnormal drug levels include malnutrition, renal impairment, drug–drug interactions, herbal supplements, and HIV or TB co‑infection affecting metabolism.

Patients may show signs of under‑dosing (persistent infection, lack of response) or over‑dosing (nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, neurotoxicity). Clinical clues are often non‑specific and require laboratory confirmation.
Key tests are drug concentration assays and organ function tests. When assays are unavailable, clinical monitoring and surrogate markers guide management.
Red flags include sudden rise in creatinine, hearing loss, or seizures. Complications are drug resistance from sub‑therapeutic levels and organ toxicity from supra‑therapeutic levels.

b: Switch to alternative with safer profile if toxicity persists
Ensure adequate hydration to protect kidneys
Avoid concurrent nephrotoxins (e.g., aminoglycosides with vancomycin)
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, adjust the dose, and monitor. Choose drugs with predictable pharmacokinetics when possible. Avoid nephrotoxic combinations and monitor renal function closely.

b: Repeat TDM 48–72 hours after dose change
Monthly renal function tests for long‑term therapy
Patient education on adherence and herbal use
sections.p: Repeat drug levels after dose change, monitor organ function, and educate patients on adherence. Preventive strategies include using fixed dosing where appropriate and avoiding herbal supplements that interfere with metabolism.
TDM is often mistaken for routine therapeutic monitoring of all drugs. It is specifically for drugs with narrow therapeutic windows or variable pharmacokinetics.
Assay interference, delayed sample processing, and patient factors (e.g., hypoalbuminemia) can give falsely low or high concentrations. Clinical context must guide interpretation.
